answers.children: Yes — Bloodhounds are good with children because their gentle nature and patient tolerance let them remain calm when toddlers tug at their long ears or use them as a pillow. Their large size as affectionate giants means they seek closeness rather than rough play, though their stubborn streak can appear if a child interrupts a scent trail. The breed’s medieval origins as trackers bred for independent work reinforce this quiet steadiness around family. (PawLabs child-friendly score: 7/10)
answers.other-pets: Yes — Bloodhounds generally get along with other pets thanks to their gentle and affectionate temperament, though their unparalleled scent-tracking drive can cause them to ignore housemates when following a trail. Same-sex tension is minimal, but their stubborn independence means introductions benefit from patience rather than force. The loose wrinkled skin and long ears that trap scent particles keep them focused on smells over social friction.
answers.exercise: Bloodhounds need one to two hours of daily exercise, ideally meandering walks that let their unmatched nose follow scent trails at their own pace. Without this they become restless and may wander miles after an invisible trail, oblivious to traffic. Their build as large scent trackers from Belgian and French forests suits mental stimulation like scent games far more than brisk power walks.
answers.shedding: Yes — Bloodhounds shed moderately year-round with their short single coat that leaves short hairs on furniture and clothing. The loose wrinkled skin and droopy jowls add to household mess beyond just hair, while the coat’s texture means loose fur sticks to fabrics rather than forming mats. Their history as medieval European trackers did not select for low-shed coats.
answers.hypoallergenic: Bloodhounds have a short, smooth coat that sheds moderately and spreads loose hair around the house. Their wrinkled skin and long ears also trap particles and contribute to a distinct scent that lingers indoors. No breed is genuinely hypoallergenic, and Bloodhounds are rarely suggested to allergy sufferers.
answers.training: No — Bloodhounds are not easy to train because their stubbornness during training and independent nature, bred for solo scent tracking over days-old trails, make them follow their nose rather than commands. Their intelligence of seven supports problem-solving on scents but not biddability, so owners must work around the breed’s medieval European roots as determined trackers that ignore calls when interested.
answers.lifespan: Bloodhounds live 10-12 years. Their large build weighing 80-110 lb and height of 23-27 in, combined with health robustness of four, means the gentle giants experience the typical demands of a heavy tracking breed developed in medieval monasteries. The short coat and loose wrinkled skin do not alter this range.
answers.size: Bloodhounds reach 80-110 lb and stand 23-27 in tall as adults. Their heavy substance as gentle giants with soulful eyes, droopy jowls and loose wrinkled skin creates a substantial presence that leans heavily for cuddles and leaves trails of slobber, making them a paradox of lazy affection and relentless investigation in daily life.
answers.barking: Bloodhounds bark moderately because their deep booming voice sounds when they are excited, frustrated or stuck from a scent they want to chase, reflecting their origins as medieval scent trackers. The breed’s stubborn independence means barking occurs more from following their nose than alerting, and the sound resonates from their large chest.
answers.apartment: No — Bloodhounds do not suit apartment living because their need for daily scent-based exercise and tendency to wander after trails conflict with confined spaces, while their booming bark carries when frustrated. The affectionate yet stubborn giants settle indoors as couch potatoes only if their unparalleled nose receives enough stimulation.
answers.first-time: No — Bloodhounds are not a good first dog because their stubbornness during training and independent drive to follow scents first demand an owner who can manage a large tracking breed without expecting quick obedience. Their gentle affectionate side is balanced by a paradox of laziness and determination that challenges novices.
